title: A People’s History of Howard Zinn
author: Ron Jacobs
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/zinnmit-680x518.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/10/a-peoples-
history-of-howard-zinn/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/zinnmit-680x518.png)

Howard Zinn giving a lecture at MIT on the Myth of American Exceptionalism.
(Screen capture from video posted to YouTube.)

Even if he had sought it out, it seems unlikely that Howard Zinn ever thought
he would achieve the fame that he came his way. This is one of the essential
lessons taken from the new biography of Zinn by Dave Zirin titled [_The People
's Historian: The Outsized Life of Howard
Zinn_.](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/724993/the-peoples-historian-
by-dave-zirin/) Zirin, who spent time on the road with Zinn several years ago
staging public conversations about history, imperialism, and more, provides an
overview worthy of the energy which defined Zinn’s life. Naturally enough, the
book begins with a survey of Zinn’s childhood as a child of immigrants living
in a section of Brooklyn crowded with newcomers to the United States, most if
not all of them working class and with little income beyond the meager wages
paid by their employers. Zinn, while correctly perceiving the existence of
economic and social inequality around him as the result of the political and
economic system in place, pursued his dreams as best as he could.

Like many young men in the United States in the early 1940s, this meant he
ended up in the military eager to fight fascism in Europe. His time as a
bombardier in the United States Army Air Force convinced him that
war—especially those between nations—was a bloodthirsty and inhumane exercise
that should be eradicated from the human species. Zirin returns to one of the
last, if not the last, bombing missions Zinn participated in. His unit was
sent to bomb a peaceful French seaside town because the generals and their
staff believed a few dozen Nazi troops remained in the village. As a result of
the bombing raid, over three thousand French civilians—thankful for what they
believed to be the end of the war—were killed.

_The People’s Historian_ tells the story of Howard Zinn’s life by highlighting
certain phases in it. Primarily a political biography, the author presents
just enough of Zinn’s personal life—his family growing up and his wife and
family as an adult—to remind the reader that politically active people also
have personal lives. By providing this reminder, Zirin encourages the reader
so inclined to become more politically involved; to risk particular comforts
for a better world. After all, Zinn certainly did exactly that. Not to stray
from where this paragraph began, let me mention a few of those parts of Zinn’s
life that Zirin highlights and were arguably the moments in his life that
informed Zinn’s politics and approach to organizing for radical change.

After gaining his first tenured teaching job at Spelman College, an all-
women’s Black college in Atlanta, Professor Zinn and his family found
themselves in the beginnings of a redirection of the movement against racial
apartheid in the US South. The text describes various actions, organizations
and individuals crucial to the movement at the time. It also emphasizes Zinn’s
rejection of any “white savior” approach and any potential paternalism that
too many allies of the movement for Black liberation fall into. Zirin writes
explicitly of the role played by Zinn and his wife Roz as participants and
organic intellectuals in the numerous direct actions, rallies and other
manifestations at the time. As it turned out, Zinn would be terminated from
the college; one assumes the administration thought the movement would die
with his departure. It’s a testament to Zinn’s organizing approach that his
firing made very little difference in terms of the movement’s growth and
successes.

While reading theis, I was reminded of a piece of advice a friend of mine gave
me during a period of organizing against the 1980s
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/zirinzinn.jpeg)](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/724993/the-
peoples-historian-by-dave-zirin/)US wars in Central America: “If you think the
revolution can’t go on without you,” this one-time CPUSA member told me. “It’s
time for you to leave the stage, refuse any more speaking engagements for a
while and go distribute leaflets on the street.” In other words, drop the
egocentrism. As the text continues to relate events in Zinn’s life, it becomes
clear that this approach was one that Zinn tried to work inside his entire
political life, even when his books were selling millions of copies. Speaking
of those books, another of the life moments Zirin uses as a springboard to
discuss his subject’s life and meaning is the success of Zinn’s _People’s
History of the United States_. Almost any honest writer will tell you the
meaning of such stratospheric success; it’s a curse and a challenge, but also
genuinely rewarding to see one's writing read by so many.

Zinn’s book titled _Vietnam: The Logic of Withdrawal_ was published in 1967.
Many groups and individuals in the growing movement against the US war in
Vietnam were only beginning to call for a negotiated end to the US war—some
were calling for a negotiated withdrawal while some were merely calling for a
negotiated peace settlement that left the US-created state of South Vietnam
intact. Zinn’s book went far beyond either of those, giving voice to a growing
element of the antiwar movement—an element composed largely of young people,
many of whom faced the reality of death in that war should the military draft
catch up with them. Like so many others opposed to the war, when I read it in
1969 as a high school freshman, it became clear that the immediate withdrawal
of all US forces from Southeast Asia was the only sane response. By 1972,
George McGovern, the Democratic Party’s nominee for US president, had made a
US withdrawal from the region within ninety days of his inauguration the
primary focus of his campaign. Anyone who knows the history of that election
knows we live in the destructive wake of the victory of McGovern’s opponent.

_The People’s Historian_ is not a biography of a great man who made history;
it's a biography of a man who encouraged the people to make history. He did so
in the classroom, the streets, meetings and more meetings, and in a life truly
lived. In doing so, one could say he became a great man. Zirin, in his always
erudite and always conversational fashion, brings that life alive, not just to
bear witness, but to remind today's readers and the readers of tomorrow that
it’s people like them who make the history Howard Zinn wrote about.
